lesson.title: Solutions: Mixing Down to the Molecular Level
lesson.summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which solute particles are dispersed down to individual molecules or ions, distinguishing it sharply from colloids and suspensions, whose larger particles scatter light or settle out.
lesson.body:
Mixtures split into two broad categories: heterogeneous, where composition varies from spot to spot, and homogeneous, where it is uniform throughout. A solution is the homogeneous case taken to its molecular extreme: solvent and solute, the roles defined a moment ago, blend so thoroughly that solute particles are dispersed as individual molecules or ions, not as visible clumps, and every sample drawn from anywhere in the solution has identical composition and properties.

That molecular extreme has a rough numerical boundary. Chemists generally place the line between a true solution and a colloid at about 1 nanometer (1 nm equals 1 × 10⁻⁹ m) and the line between a colloid and a coarse suspension at about 1000 nm, roughly the size of a single bacterium. A dissolved chloride ion is only about 0.2 nm across. Dividing 1000 nm by 0.2 nm gives 5000, meaning that ion is about five thousand times smaller than the threshold for a suspension, which is exactly why it never settles to the bottom of a glass and passes straight through any filter paper. Colloids, like milk or fog, sit in between: their particles are large enough to scatter light visibly, the Tyndall effect, but still too small to settle out on their own.

True solutions do not scatter light noticeably, do not separate under gravity, and cannot be pulled apart by ordinary filtration, because there is nothing coarse enough for the filter to catch. All of that follows directly from the particles being individual molecules or ions rather than clusters.

Solutions exist across every combination of phases, not just solids dissolved in liquids. Air is a solution of gases, mostly oxygen dissolved throughout nitrogen, with no solvent-solute distinction that matters much since both are gases. Brass is a solid solution of zinc dissolved in copper. Saline is the familiar case, a solid ionic solute dissolved in a liquid solvent. In every case, the solute and solvent vocabulary from the previous chapter still applies.

Because a dissolved solute is broken all the way down to individual particles, its amount per volume of solution can be counted precisely, in moles, not just estimated as "a little" or "a lot." That precise counting is exactly what concentration units and molarity are built to do.
